a type defines a kind of thing. its definition is `type/<name>.md`, and its instances live in `type/<name>/`. the schema for a type definition is [type.schema.json](type.schema.json).

## base

every instance of every type has the okf base. okf requires only `type`; the rest is optional:

- **identity**: `type`, `title`, `description`.
- **provenance**: `sources[]`, `usage_window`.
- **trust**: `generated: {by, at}`, `verified[]`.
- **lifecycle**: `status`, `stale_after`.

## definition

every type states:

- **type**: `type`.
- **title**: its name. instances carry it as their `type` in frontmatter.
- **fields**: the frontmatter every instance must have, beyond `type`.
- **owns**: the paths each instance creates and manages fully. every path has exactly one owner.
- **writes**: the paths each instance modifies without owning them.

==> type/decision.md <==
---
type: type
title: decision
description: a choice and why it was made, written once.
fields: [type, title, status]
owns: [type/decision/<nnnn>-<name>.md]
writes: [DECISIONS.md]
---

# decision

a decision records a choice and why. it is written once and never edited.

- **status**: `proposed`, `accepted` or `superseded`.
- **supersedes**: optional, the number of the decision this one replaces.

to change a decision, write a new one that supersedes it. `DECISIONS.md` is derived from the instances and never edited by hand.

==> type/rule.md <==
---
type: type
title: rule
description: a constraint that can be checked, enforcing a decision.
fields: [type, title, applies_to]
owns: [type/rule/<name>.md]
watches: [<applies_to>]
---

# rule

a rule is a decision made checkable.

- **applies_to**: the paths the rule constrains. the rule watches them and is re-checked when they change.
- **from**: optional, the decision it enforces.

a "we do X" that cannot be checked is a decision, not a rule.

==> type/trigger.md <==
---
type: type
title: trigger
description: a script that runs when a file changes or an event happens.
fields: [type, title, when]
owns: [type/trigger/<name>.md, scripts/trigger/<name>.sh]
watches: [<when>]
---

# trigger

a trigger `<name>` owns:

- `type/trigger/<name>.md`: the instance.
- `scripts/trigger/<name>.sh`: what runs.

- **when**: the paths or events that run the script.

the base `watches` field is the simplest trigger: it marks interest in a path and runs nothing. a trigger adds the script.

---
type: type
title: tool
description: an executable skogai uses, with its wrapper, scripts and workflow.
fields: [type, title]
owns: [type/tool/<name>.md, bin/<name>, scripts/<name>/, workflows/<name>.md]
---

a tool `<name>` owns:

- `type/tool/<name>.md`: the instance, and its documentation.
- `bin/<name>`: the entrypoint.
- `scripts/<name>/`: everything the entrypoint calls.
- `workflows/<name>.md`: how and when to use it.

# config

a config is a [git config](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#_configuration_file) file of `section.key = value` pairs, read and written with `skogai config`.

## layers

folded in order, later wins:

1. **base**: `config` in dash. the defaults.
2. **global**: `~/.skogai/config`, or `$SKOGAI_GLOBAL_CONFIG`.
3. **local**: `<repo>/.skogai/config`, or `$SKOGAI_LOCAL_CONFIG`.
4. **file**: with `--file x.md` (repeatable), the frontmatter of `x.md`, then of `x.local.md`. nested keys flatten to `a.b.c`, `_` reads as `-`, and `--scope s` mounts them under `s.`. needs `yq`.
5. **env**: key `a.b-c` reads env `SKOGAI_A_BC`, which overrides every layer. `.` is a relation and becomes `_`; `-` is part of a name and is dropped.

## commands

- `skogai config get <key> [--show-origin] [--file x.md]... [--scope s]`: exit `1` if unset, `2` if a layer can't be read. a list prints one item per line.
- `skogai config set <key> <value> [--global | --file x.md [--scope s]]`: writes local unless `--global`. `--file` writes `x.local.md`, never `x.md`; the value is read as yaml.
- `skogai config unset <key> [--global | --file x.md [--scope s]]`
- `skogai config list [--show-origin] [--file x.md]... [--scope s]`: a list prints one line per item.
- `skogai config env [--file x.md]... [--scope s]`: the resolved config as `export` lines, for `mise` `_.source` or `eval`. a list's items are newline-separated.
- `skogai config files [--file x.md]...`: the path of each layer, and whether it exists.

# router

a router routes, it does not hold content. its body is one `<routes>` block: the frontmatter `type` names the block, as `router` names `<routes>`.

```markdown
---
type: router
title: dash-skogai
---

<routes>

- @type/index.md - small index, loaded with the router
- tmp/ - untyped or undecided, read when needed

</routes>
```

- **entries**: one per line, `- <path> [- <description>]`. the description lets an agent decide without opening the file.
- **`@path`**: loaded with the router. use it for small routers and indexes.
- **plain path**: listed, read on demand. use it for anything with real content.

# skogai

the cli that turns dash into a dot. it is a function over values: `check` and `plan` are pure, and `apply` is the only writer.

## values

- **dash**: type definitions and functions, named by ref and resolved to a commit at use.
- **layers**: `base` (dash@ref), `global` (`~/.skogai`), `local` (`<repo>/.skogai`). key/value settings use [config](../config.md).
- **resolved**: `fold(merge, [base, global, local])`, later layer wins.
- **dot**: the resolved value written to disk, a closed union of skogai types.

## commands

### `skogai config`

implemented in `bin/skogai`. see [config](../config.md).

### `skogai check [<dot>]`

pure. reports type errors, writes nothing.

1. runs `okn validate` on the dot.
2. every file has exactly one owner (see [type](../type.md#check)).
3. every `type` tag is a case dash defines, and the file has that case's `fields`.
4. every derived file equals its regeneration.

prints the dash ref and the commit it resolved to.

### `skogai resolve [<dot>]`

pure. prints the resolved value, and for each entry the layer it came from.

### `skogai plan [<dot>]`

pure. prints the patch `apply` would make, as a git diff. an empty patch means the dot is already up to date.

### `skogai apply [<dot>] [<patch>]`

the only writer. applies `<patch>`, or the output of `plan` if none is given, with `git apply`.

- idempotent: after `apply`, `plan` is empty.
- init is `apply` on an empty dot.
- moving to a newer dash is changing the ref, then `plan` and `apply`.

## conventions

- `<dot>` defaults to `./.skogai`.
- output goes to stdout, diagnostics to stderr.
- exit `0`: clean or empty patch. `1`: type errors or a non-empty patch. `2`: usage or internal error.
- `--json` on every command, for machine output.
- anything okn already does (list, search, view, validate) is called through okn, not rebuilt.

## open

see [TODO](../../TODO.md): where the dash ref is recorded, merge semantics per field, and how a type declares a derived file.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Appends one row to the event log for an event we acted upon.
# Skips the row when the settings (see settings.sh) switch the plugin off or
# leave the event out of `events`.
# Usage: <hook stdin json> | append-json.sh [what we did]
set -euo pipefail

input=$(cat)
cwd=$(jq -r '.cwd // empty' <<<"$input")
cwd=${cwd:-$PWD}
root=$(git -C "$cwd" rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null || echo "$cwd")
. "$(dirname "$0")/settings.sh"
[[ $SKOGAI_ENABLED == true ]] || exit 0
skogai_logs "$(jq -r '.hook_event_name // empty' <<<"$input")" || exit 0
log=$SKOGAI_LOG
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$log")"

# Hooks can fire in parallel (PreToolUse for parallel tool calls), so hold a
# lock on the log while the row is written.
exec 9>>"$log"
flock 9
jq -c --arg ts "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3NZ)" --arg action "${1:-}" \
  '{ts: $ts, event: .hook_event_name}
   + (if $action == "" then {} else {action: $action} end)
   + {input: .}' <<<"$input" >&9

# router

a router routes, it does not hold content. its body is one `<routes>` block: the frontmatter `type` names the block, as `router` names `<routes>`.

```markdown
---
type: router
title: dash-skogai
---

<routes>

- @type/index.md - small index, loaded with the router
- tmp/ - untyped or undecided, read when needed

</routes>
```

- **entries**: one per line, `- <path> [- <description>]`. the description lets an agent decide without opening the file.
- **`@path`**: loaded with the router. use it for small routers and indexes.
- **plain path**: listed, read on demand. use it for anything with real content.
- **no transitive bloat**: a router never `@`-links a file that itself `@`-links content. that loads everything below it.
- **one step**: each router points to the next level, never to everything.

## CLAUDE.md

claude code loads only `CLAUDE.md`, never `SKOGAI.md`. so each router also owns the `CLAUDE.md` next to it, and that file is derived: its whole content is

```markdown
@SKOGAI.md
```

it is never hand-edited, and `check` regenerates and compares it. routes go in `SKOGAI.md`, not in `CLAUDE.md`.

the source this was folded from is [tmp/routing](../tmp/routing/README.md).

# skogai

how an agent runs [skogai](../type/tool/skogai.md) until `bin/skogai` has the command. `bin/skogai` has only `config` so far. each section is one command, written as a prompt: hand an agent this file and the command name.

paths are relative to the dash root, the folder holding `type/`. `<dot>` is the dot to check. in this repo it is `src`, later `./.skogai`.

## check

pure. reports type errors, writes nothing. safe to run unattended.

do not edit, create or delete any file. if something looks fixable, report it; do not fix it.

run each command exactly as written, one per shell call, from the dash root: no `cd`, `&&`, `;` or pipes. an unattended run allows only these commands, so a chained one is denied.

1. **ref**: run `git rev-parse HEAD` and `git status --porcelain type/`. report the commit, and `dirty` if `type/` has uncommitted changes.
2. **okn**: run `okn validate <dot>`. every okn error is a check error.
3. **cases**: read every `type/<name>.md`. a file whose frontmatter has `type: type` is a case: its `title` is the tag, with its `fields` and `owns`. a file without that frontmatter is a stub: report it as a warning, not a case.
4. **files**: list every file in `<dot>` with `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard <dot>`.
5. **owners**: for each file, find the cases whose `owns` patterns match its path relative to `<dot>`. `<name>` matches one path segment, and a pattern ending in `/` matches everything under it.
   - no owner: `untyped`.
   - two or more owners: `conflict`, naming the owners.
6. **tags**: for each `.md` file, read its frontmatter.
   - no `type`: `untagged`.
   - a `type` that is not a case: `unknown tag`.
   - a field from the case's `fields` missing: `missing field`.
7. **derived**: skip. how a type declares a derived file is still open (see [TODO](../TODO.md)). say it was skipped.

### output

one line per finding, then a summary:

```text
error   <path>: untyped
error   <path>: unknown tag "index"
warning type/task.md: stub, no frontmatter
skipped derived files: not specified
dash    <commit> [dirty]
result  errors=<n> warnings=<n>
```

`result errors=0` is clean. do not add advice after the summary.

# event

an event is something that happened, such as a turn ending or a tool about to run. each time it happens, one row is appended to the event log. rows are never edited; the log as a whole is temporary and can be deleted.

an event `<name>` owns:

- `type/event/<name>.md`: the instance. it says what happened and when it fires.
- `type/event/<name>.schema.json`: its rows. it narrows the row in [event.schema.json](event.schema.json) to this event's `input`.
- `scripts/event/<name>.sh`: what runs when it happens.

- **enabled**: optional. an event runs only when this is `true`. missing, or no instance at all, is off.

## the row

one json object per line in `.skogai/logs/event.jsonl`:

- **ts**: when it happened, utc, to the millisecond.
- **event**: the instance's `title`.
- **action**: optional, what the script did, when it did more than record the row.
- **input**: everything the event came with, unchanged.

## the script

`scripts/event/<name>.sh` gets the event's `input` and appends exactly one row. it may answer: go on, stop with a reason, or a structured answer the event's source understands. when it can't run, it says so and lets the event go on, so a broken script never stops work.

## defaults

no event is on. the log path is the base config key `event.log-path`.

A1 and A2 are drafted in `~/skogai/dash-skogai`, left uncommitted for you to review. `event.log-path` resolves from the base config; I haven't run `dash:check` yet.

**A1: `type/event.md`**
- **What an event is:** "something that happened, recorded as one row appended to the event log." Rows are never edited, and the log as a whole is temporary.
- **What each event owns:** `type/event/<name>.md`, `type/event/<name>.schema.json` and `scripts/event/<name>.sh`. Every event writes `.skogai/logs/event.jsonl`.
- **Opt-in:** an optional `enabled` field. An event runs only when it is `true`; if it is missing, or the event has no file, the event is off.
- **The script:** it gets the event's input and appends exactly one row. It may answer "go on", "stop, with a reason", or a structured answer the source understands. If it can't run, it says so and lets the event go on.
- **No mechanisms:** the definition doesn't mention Claude Code hooks, exit codes, jq or flock. Those belong in the plugin.
- **No `watches`:** I left out the type-level `watches` the workorder mentioned. Nothing watches on behalf of every event, so a single event can add its own (`Stop` reads the log, for example).

**A2: `type/event.schema.json`**
I followed the existing convention, where `type.schema.json` is the schema for every type definition. So `event.schema.json` is the schema for event files (`type`, `title`, `enabled`, …). The row format is a shared definition inside it, `$defs/row`: `{ts, event, action?, input}`, with `input` passed through unchanged. Each `<Name>.schema.json` in A3 will build on it and narrow `input` to that event.

# skogai

how an agent runs [skogai](../type/tool/skogai.md) until `bin/skogai` has the command. `bin/skogai` has only `config` so far. each section is one command, written as a prompt: hand an agent this file and the command name.

paths are relative to the dash root, the folder holding `type/`. `<dot>` is the dot to check. in this repo it is `src`, later `./.skogai`.

## check

pure. reports type errors, writes nothing. safe to run unattended.

do not edit, create or delete any file. if something looks fixable, report it; do not fix it.

run each command exactly as written, one per shell call, from the dash root: no `cd`, `&&`, `;` or pipes. an unattended run allows only these commands, so a chained one is denied.

1. **ref**: run `git rev-parse HEAD` and `git status --porcelain type/`. report the commit, and `dirty` if `type/` has uncommitted changes.
2. **okn**: run `okn validate <dot>`. every okn error is a check error.
3. **cases**: read every `type/<name>.md`. a file whose frontmatter has `type: type` is a case: its `title` is the tag, with its `fields` and `owns`. a file without that frontmatter is a stub: report it as a warning, not a case.
4. **files**: list every file in `<dot>` with `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard <dot>`.
5. **owners**: for each file, find the cases whose `owns` patterns match its path relative to `<dot>`. `<name>` matches one path segment, and a pattern ending in `/` matches everything under it.
   - no owner: `untyped`.
   - two or more owners: `conflict`, naming the owners.
6. **tags**: for each `.md` file, read its frontmatter.
   - no `type`: `untagged`.
   - a `type` that is not a case: `unknown tag`.
   - a field from the case's `fields` missing: `missing field`.
7. **derived**: skip. how a type declares a derived file is still open (see [TODO](../TODO.md)). say it was skipped.

### output

one line per finding, then a summary:

```text
error   <path>: untyped
error   <path>: unknown tag "index"
warning type/task.md: stub, no frontmatter
skipped derived files: not specified
dash    <commit> [dirty]
result  errors=<n> warnings=<n>
```

`result errors=0` is clean. do not add advice after the summary.

## plan

not written yet. depends on where a dot records its dash ref and how layers merge (see [TODO](../TODO.md)).

## apply

not written yet. the only writer: needs human approval, never automated.

---
type: type
title: type
description: a kind of thing, and the files each of its instances owns, writes and watches.
fields: [type, title, description, fields, owns, writes, watches]
owns: [type/<name>.md, type/<name>.schema.json]
---

# type

a type defines a kind of thing. its definition is `type/<name>.md`, its instances live in `type/<name>/`, and `type/<name>.schema.json`, when there is one, is the schema for those instances. so [type.schema.json](type.schema.json) is the schema for every type definition.

## base

every instance of every type has the okf base. okf requires only `type`; the rest is optional:

- **identity**: `type`, `title`, `description`.
- **provenance**: `sources[]`, `usage_window`.
- **trust**: `generated: {by, at}`, `verified[]`.
- **lifecycle**: `status`, `stale_after`.

## definition

every type states:

- **type**: `type`.
- **title**: its name. instances carry it as their `type` in frontmatter.
- **fields**: the frontmatter every instance must have, beyond `type`.
- **owns**: the paths each instance creates and manages fully. every path has exactly one owner.
- **writes**: the paths each instance modifies without owning them.
- **watches**: the paths each instance reads and wants to know about when they change.

`<name>` in a path is the instance's name. a path ending in `/` is a folder.

## check

- a file with no owner is untyped: an error.
- a file with two owners is a conflict: an error.
- ownership is one step. `type` owns `type/tool.md`; `tool` owns `type/tool/gita.md`. `type` never owns what is under `type/tool/`.
- `writes` and `watches` can overlap freely.

`type` is itself a type: every `type/<name>.md` is an instance of it, including this file.

---
type: type
title: decision
description: a choice and why it was made, written once.
fields: [type, title, status]
owns: [type/decision/<nnnn>-<name>.md]
writes: [DECISIONS.md]
---

# decision

a decision records a choice and why. it is written once and never edited.

- **status**: `proposed`, `accepted` or `superseded`.
- **supersedes**: optional, the number of the decision this one replaces.

to change a decision, write a new one that supersedes it. `DECISIONS.md` is derived from the instances and never edited by hand.

---
type: type
title: rule
description: a constraint that can be checked, enforcing a decision.
fields: [type, title, applies_to]
owns: [type/rule/<name>.md]
watches: [<applies_to>]
---

# rule

a rule is a decision made checkable.

- **applies_to**: the paths the rule constrains. the rule watches them and is re-checked when they change.
- **from**: optional, the decision it enforces.

a "we do X" that cannot be checked is a decision, not a rule.

---
type: type
title: trigger
description: a script that runs when a file changes or an event happens.
fields: [type, title, when]
owns: [type/trigger/<name>.md, scripts/trigger/<name>.sh]
watches: [<when>]
---

# trigger

a trigger `<name>` owns:

- `type/trigger/<name>.md`: the instance.
- `scripts/trigger/<name>.sh`: what runs.

- **when**: the paths or events that run the script.

the base `watches` field is the simplest trigger: it marks interest in a path and runs nothing. a trigger adds the script.

---
type: type
title: tool
description: an executable skogai uses, with its wrapper, scripts and workflow.
fields: [type, title]
owns: [type/tool/<name>.md, bin/<name>, scripts/<name>/, workflows/<name>.md]
---

# tool

instances: [herdr](tool/herdr.md), [wt](tool/wt.md), [gita](tool/gita.md), [mise](tool/mise.md), [okn](tool/okn.md), [skogai](tool/skogai.md).

a tool `<name>` owns:

- `type/tool/<name>.md`: the instance, and its documentation.
- `bin/<name>`: the entrypoint.
- `scripts/<name>/`: everything the entrypoint calls.
- `workflows/<name>.md`: how and when to use it.
# task
# knowledge
# memory
# repo
# spec

---
type: type
title: config
description: key/value settings, folded across the base, global and local layers.
fields: [type, title]
owns: [config]
---

# config

a config is a [git config](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#_configuration_file) file of `section.key = value` pairs, read and written with `skogai config`.

## layers

folded in order, later wins:

1. **base**: `config` in dash. the defaults.
2. **global**: `~/.skogai/config`, or `$SKOGAI_GLOBAL_CONFIG`.
3. **local**: `<repo>/.skogai/config`, or `$SKOGAI_LOCAL_CONFIG`.
4. **file**: with `--file x.md` (repeatable), the frontmatter of `x.md`, then of `x.local.md`. nested keys flatten to `a.b.c`, `_` reads as `-`, and `--scope s` mounts them under `s.`. needs `yq`.
5. **env**: key `a.b-c` reads env `SKOGAI_A_BC`, which overrides every layer. `.` is a relation and becomes `_`; `-` is part of a name and is dropped.

## commands

- `skogai config get <key> [--show-origin] [--file x.md]... [--scope s]`: exit `1` if unset, `2` if a layer can't be read. a list prints one item per line.
- `skogai config set <key> <value> [--global | --file x.md [--scope s]]`: writes local unless `--global`. `--file` writes `x.local.md`, never `x.md`; the value is read as yaml.
- `skogai config unset <key> [--global | --file x.md [--scope s]]`
- `skogai config list [--show-origin] [--file x.md]... [--scope s]`: a list prints one line per item.
- `skogai config env [--file x.md]... [--scope s]`: the resolved config as `export` lines, for `mise` `_.source` or `eval`. a list's items are newline-separated.
- `skogai config files [--file x.md]...`: the path of each layer, and whether it exists.

## merge

every key is replaced by the later layer. a key set twice in one layer resolves to its last value.

in a file layer, a frontmatter list is one value, replaced whole. `null` (`~`) removes the key, so it falls through to the default.

## keys

- `stage.on-stop`, `commit.on-stop`, `merge.on-stop`: git automation on stop.
- `stage.on-user-prompt-submit`, `commit.on-user-prompt-submit`, `merge.on-user-prompt-submit`: git automation on prompt submit.

---
type: type
title: event
description: something that happened, recorded as one row appended to the event log.
fields: [type, title]
owns: [type/event/<name>.md, type/event/<name>.schema.json, scripts/event/<name>.sh]
writes: [.skogai/logs/event.jsonl]
---

# event

an event is something that happened, such as a turn ending or a tool about to run. each time it happens, one row is appended to the event log. rows are never edited; the log as a whole is temporary and can be deleted.

an event `<name>` owns:

- `type/event/<name>.md`: the instance. it says what happened and when it fires.
- `type/event/<name>.schema.json`: its rows. it narrows the row in [event.schema.json](event.schema.json) to this event's `input`.
- `scripts/event/<name>.sh`: what runs when it happens.

- **enabled**: optional. an event runs only when this is `true`. missing, or no instance at all, is off.

## the row

one json object per line in `.skogai/logs/event.jsonl`:

- **ts**: when it happened, utc, to the millisecond.
- **event**: the instance's `title`.
- **action**: optional, what the script did, when it did more than record the row.
- **input**: everything the event came with, unchanged. `$defs/input` in the schema lists the fields every event shares; `type/event/<name>.schema.json` adds its own and says which are required.

## the script

`scripts/event/<name>.sh` gets the event's `input` and appends exactly one row. it may answer: go on, stop with a reason, or a structured answer the event's source understands. when it can't run, it says so and lets the event go on, so a broken script never stops work.

## defaults

no event is on. the log path is the base config key `event.log-path`.

---
type: type
title: router
description: a file that points to other files, so an agent loads only what the task needs.
status: draft
fields: [type, title]
owns: [<name>/SKOGAI.md, <name>/CLAUDE.md]
---

# router

a router routes, it does not hold content. its body is one `<routes>` block: the frontmatter `type` names the block, as `router` names `<routes>`.

```markdown
---
type: router
title: dash-skogai
---

<routes>

- @type/index.md - small index, loaded with the router
- tmp/ - untyped or undecided, read when needed

</routes>
```

- **entries**: one per line, `- <path> [- <description>]`. the description lets an agent decide without opening the file.
- **`@path`**: loaded with the router. use it for small routers and indexes.
- **plain path**: listed, read on demand. use it for anything with real content.
- **no transitive bloat**: a router never `@`-links a file that itself `@`-links content. that loads everything below it.
- **one step**: each router points to the next level, never to everything.

## CLAUDE.md

claude code loads only `CLAUDE.md`, never `SKOGAI.md`. so each router also owns the `CLAUDE.md` next to it, and that file is derived: its whole content is

```markdown
@SKOGAI.md
```

it is never hand-edited, and `check` regenerates and compares it. routes go in `SKOGAI.md`, not in `CLAUDE.md`.

the source this was folded from is [tmp/routing](../tmp/routing/README.md).

# type

one file per type. a type defines its instances and the files each instance owns, writes and watches.

- [type](type.md)
- [decision](decision.md)
- [rule](rule.md)
- [trigger](trigger.md)
- [tool](tool.md)
- [task](task.md)
- [knowledge](knowledge.md)
- [memory](memory.md)
- [repo](repo.md)
- [spec](spec.md)
- [config](config.md)
- [event](event.md)
- [router](router.md)

---
type: index
corpus_schema:
  version: "1"
  document_types:
    - id: draft
      paths: ["*.md"]
      required: [title]
    - id: tool
      paths: ["tools/**"]
      required: [title]
---

# src

the future dot: authored source that `apply` turns into a `.skogai`.

--- ORCHESTRATOR.md
# Orchestrator — design notes

Status: draft, 2026-10-14. This is something to work from, not a decision.

What a setup is, its files, run options and commands are in
[FEATURES.md](../claude-code/FEATURES.md). This file covers only what is
specific to the orchestrator.

## Where it lives

`setup/` here is a relative symlink to `../claude-code/setups/orchestration`,
which holds the real `append-system-prompt.md` and `settings.json`. Editing
through either path changes the same file. A folder symlink is used because
git stores symlinks but not hard links: hard-linked copies became independent
files on checkout.

Why: the main session imports the same prompt the harness tests, so we
iterate on our own setup by using it. A change shows up on the next
`/clear` with no harness run in between.

The prompt gets used in two ways:

| Where | How the prompt arrives | `settings.json` |
|---|---|---|
| This repo's main session | `@` import through `CLAUDE.md`, so as project instructions rather than system prompt | not applied, only listed |
| The harness (`SETUP=orchestration bin/agent`) | `--append-system-prompt-file` | applied (same as baseline) |

## The prompt today

Role only: discuss, decide, delegate and review, and workers do the bulk
of the work. It says nothing yet about *how* to delegate.

## Parked: parts that were in the prompt

These were cut down to the role. Each one comes back once there is
something real behind it.

| Part | Why it was there | Blocked on / what's needed first |
|---|---|---|

# Orchestration — plan

Status: draft, 2026-10-14. The first pieces exist in `projects/claude-code`.
Open work is tracked in [TODO.md](TODO.md).

## Goal

skogai is the orchestration layer. The main session discusses things with
skogix and decides. It uses tools and other agents to do the bulk of the
work: implementing, researching, reading and summarizing.

## Scope of this folder

`projects/orchestration/` holds only what has been discussed and is
active. `wip/` is temporary and still being tested. Something moves from
`wip/` into here only after we discuss it and adopt it.

## Big picture

`projects/claude-code` is the collection of Claude Code setups, and also
the test bed for orchestration. The orchestrator is the agent that does
what we have been doing by hand: it spawns other setups.

| Orchestration idea | What it is in `projects/claude-code` |
|---|---|
| Worker kind or role | A setup, e.g. `commit-msg`, later `reviewer` or `implementer` |
| Handoff contract v0 | `bin/agent`: prompt in on stdin, one message out on stdout |
| Proof that a worker is good | Its cases and evals. A setup is tested before it is relied on |
| The orchestrator | A setup too (`orchestration`). Its main tool is "run setup X with this prompt" |
| `TOOLS.md` | Mostly the list of setups: what each one is for and when to use it |

Example from 2026-10-14: instead of the orchestrator reading a worker's
diff and writing the commit message, it should spawn a `reviewer` setup and
the existing `commit-msg` setup, then read only their replies. Its context
stays on the discussion.

This also addresses the "tools went unused" problem. The orchestrator has
few tools, spawning setups is the main one, and each setup is improved on
its own through its evals.

## The handoff contract (v0)

```
input:  a prompt (plain text)
output: a message back (plain text)
```

`bin/agent` already does this for one-shot workers. Workorder files,
worktrees and merging come later and build on it.

## Lessons

- **Tools we had went unused.** That made most of the earlier work useless
  in the end. Every tool we rely on is documented in `TOOLS.md`, and if a
  tool isn't documented, we don't count on it.
- **First herdr handoff (2026-10-14).** A `claude` worker in a herdr pane
  made the `append-system-prompt.md` change in `projects/claude-code`. It
  worked, but with `acceptEdits` it still stopped for approval on every
  shell command.
- **Harness gaps found by that worker.** `TOOLS` defaults to none, so the
  orchestration setup has no `Agent` tool. The sandbox doesn't contain
  `TOOLS.md` or the repo.

## Open questions

- Which parts of `wip/dot-dash-skogai` decisions 0002 (orchestration model)
  and 0003 (repo roles) still hold? 0002's workorders and herdr/`wt`
  workers look like the long-running worker kind.
- The `Agent` tool is kept as a fallback when no setup fits. Is that
  enough, or should it be removed so missing setups are always noticed?

---
name: herdr
description: "Control Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for coding agents. Use only when the user explicitly mentions Herdr or asks to use Herdr to inspect or control panes, tabs, workspaces, commands, or another agent. Do not use merely because a task could benefit from a background terminal, delegation, or parallel work. Requires HERDR_ENV=1."
---

# Herdr

Herdr organizes terminals into workspaces, tabs, and panes, recognizes coding agents running inside panes, and exposes the current session through the `herdr` CLI.

Before issuing any control command, verify that this agent is running inside a Herdr-managed pane:

```bash
test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1
```

If the check fails, say that you are not running inside Herdr and stop. Do not inspect or control the focused Herdr session from outside Herdr.

When the check passes, the `herdr` binary in `PATH` talks to the current session. Use it to inspect neighboring work, create terminal layout, start agents and commands, read output, and wait for state changes.

## Learn the current CLI

The installed binary is the authority for command syntax. Start with:

```bash
herdr --help
```

Then print the relevant command group by running the group without a subcommand:

```bash
herdr agent
herdr pane
herdr workspace
herdr tab
herdr worktree
herdr terminal
herdr notification
herdr integration
herdr session
herdr machine
```

Do not run bare `herdr` for discovery; it launches or attaches the TUI. Do not probe a mutating nested command by omitting arguments. Commands such as `herdr workspace create` are valid with defaults and will execute.

Most control commands return JSON. Read identifiers and state from those responses instead of predicting them.

## Understand layout, panes, and agents

Choose the primitive that matches the job:

- Workspace, tab, and pane topology organize terminal locations.
- Pane commands control raw terminals, shells, tests, servers, input, and output.
- Agent commands control the recognized coding agent currently occupying a pane.

A pane exists whether or not it contains an agent. `agent start` requires an existing available shell pane and never creates, splits, or moves layout. Use pane commands for ordinary processes. Use agent commands when Herdr must validate agent identity or interpret `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done`, and `unknown` lifecycle states.

Agent commands accept either a unique live agent name or the pane ID currently hosting that agent. They do not accept terminal IDs or bare agent-kind labels. Names must match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}` and be unique among live agents. A name follows the current pane occupant and is cleared when that agent exits, is released, or is replaced. Suspending an agent with Ctrl+Z and running a non-agent command preserves its identity while the exact process remains alive. This does not preserve the original identity across another recognized agent taking over. A retained identity does not mean the agent is in the foreground; inspect the pane before sending input.

`idle` and `done` normally indicate the agent is ready for input; neither guarantees that an unfamiliar approval dialog was recognized or that a retained agent is in the foreground. The CLI/API uses the server's seen state to distinguish them; explicit focus commands mark the target seen, while reads do not. Each TUI client tracks viewed completions independently, so its Done badge can differ from the CLI or another client's badge. Antigravity and Grok can be idle while background tasks or subagents keep running, so a settled-state wait is not proof those jobs have finished. `blocked` means Herdr recognized an approval or question UI. `unknown` means an agent is present but Herdr cannot classify it confidently; it does not prove completion.

## Use IDs and caller context

Public IDs are opaque stable handles:

- workspace: `w1`
- tab: `w1:t1`
- pane: `w1:p1`

Closed tab and pane IDs are not reused. A pane moved into another workspace receives a new workspace-qualified pane ID. After `pane move`, continue with `.result.move_result.pane.pane_id` or the live agent name. The old value is reported as `.result.move_result.previous_pane_id`; only the moved process's inherited caller context keeps resolving that old ID, so do not use it as a general agent target.

Herdr injects the caller's context into each managed pane:

```bash
printf '%s\n' "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID" "$HERDR_TAB_ID" "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Prefer `--current` when a pane command should target the calling pane. An omitted `pane split` target uses the calling pane when `HERDR_PANE_ID` is available, otherwise the focused pane. Other commands may use the UI-focused pane, which can belong to the user or another client.

Discover live state with:

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr tab list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr pane current --current
herdr pane list --workspace "$HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID"
herdr agent list
```

Creation responses expose the IDs to use next. `workspace create` returns `.result.workspace`, `.result.tab`, and `.result.root_pane`. `tab create` returns `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`. `pane split` returns the new pane as `.result.pane`.

IDs and live agent names are scoped to one server. Two saved SSH machines can both have `w1:p1` or an agent named `reviewer`. Selecting a machine in the TUI does not retarget commands running in your pane: without `--machine`, they still use the inherited session and socket context.

To control a saved SSH machine, use the same global prefix for discovery and every later command:

```bash
herdr --machine <label-or-id> agent list
herdr --machine <label-or-id> pane list
herdr --machine <label-or-id> agent prompt <remote-agent-name> "Reply with your current status." --wait --timeout 120000
```

The selector must be an enabled saved profile ID or a unique, case-sensitive label, not an arbitrary SSH hostname. Commands use that profile's remote session without an open TUI. Do not combine `--machine` with `--session` or `--remote`. Discover IDs on that machine; inherited local IDs and `--current` do not identify remote panes.

Both installations must support machine API forwarding, and the remote server must already be running and API-compatible. Forwarding never installs, starts, or restarts a server and never falls back to Local. Local configuration, session management, installation commands, and interactive attachment are not forwarded. Remote worktree paths must be absolute, `~`, or start with `~/`; plugin link paths must be absolute. A connection failure does not prove a mutation was not applied: inspect remote state before retrying.

`herdr machine list` lists saved connection profiles, not a cross-machine pane inventory; add `--json` for scripts. Only add, remove, enable, or disable profiles when the user asks. Removing a profile disconnects the client but does not stop remote sessions. Interactive `machine add` discovers running remote sessions and may ask the user to pick one; non-interactive setup uses the remote default session unless `--remote-session` is explicitly supplied. Use `herdr machine status [<label-or-id>] --json` to diagnose a failing machine. `herdr machine reconnect` needs the user to complete SSH authentication in their terminal; do not run it for them. Setup asks before stopping an incompatible server and defaults to No; do not approve replacement without the user's consent. Experimental handoff is not part of `machine add`.

## Start and coordinate an agent

Default to a sibling pane in the current tab and the current working directory. Do not create a workspace, tab, worktree, or different cwd unless the user explicitly requests that topology or location.

Honor a direction requested by the user. Otherwise inspect the caller pane:

```bash
herdr pane layout --pane "$HERDR_PANE_ID"
```

Split a wide pane to the right and a narrow or tall pane down. Avoid repeated same-direction splits that create unusably narrow columns or short rows. Keep the user's focus in the calling pane and explicitly preserve the caller's working directory:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Replace `right` with `down` when appropriate. Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`.

An available shell pane must be at its interactive prompt, with the shell itself in the foreground and no foreground command, editor, or agent running. Start a supported agent in that pane with a useful unique name:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id>
```

Use the kind requested by the user. Run `herdr agent` to inspect the installed kind list and options. Pass native agent arguments only after `--`:

```bash
herdr agent start reviewer --kind codex --pane <returned-pane-id> -- <agent-args...>
```

A successful `agent start` returns only after Herdr detects the expected agent in the same pane and considers it ready for interactive input. If the agent is blocked during startup, the command returns `agent_not_ready` immediately but keeps the name available for `agent read` and `agent send-keys`. Wait until the agent becomes idle before prompting it. Startup defaults to a 30-second timeout.

Submit work through the agent surface:

```bash
herdr agent prompt reviewer "Review the current diff and report only actionable findings." --wait --timeout 120000
```

`agent prompt` honors the pane's live bracketed-paste mode and sends text followed by encoded Enter as one ordered submission. It reports successful submission only after both have been written; that alone does not prove the agent started a turn. For Codex on Windows, Herdr sends a paste boundary before Enter so submission does not depend on prompt size. It rejects an agent already waiting at an approval or question dialog with `agent_blocked` before sending any input. Inspect the blocked UI and ask the user before answering it. For normal agent work, `--wait` is enough: it waits for the first settled `idle`, `done`, or `blocked` state. Do not repeat those defaults with `--until`.

With `--wait`, a prompt sent from a non-working state must produce observed `working` or `blocked` activity. After submission, Herdr waits up to five seconds for that activity; unrelated `idle`, `done`, or session changes do not satisfy this gate. It returns `agent_prompt_stalled` if no activity is observed, or `timeout` if the caller's timeout expires first. The caller timeout includes submission time. Without a timeout, the settled-state wait is indefinite after activity is observed. This wait tracks lifecycle state, not an individual turn; if the agent is already working, completion of the active turn may satisfy it.

Use `--until` only for a state-specific workflow, such as waiting for an already-running agent to request input:

```bash
herdr agent wait reviewer --until blocked --timeout 120000
```

Without `--until`, standalone `agent wait` uses the same settled-state defaults as `agent prompt --wait`.

Use logical keys for interactive agent UI controls:

```bash
herdr agent send-keys reviewer esc
herdr agent send-keys reviewer ctrl+c
```

Herdr validates all keys before writing any bytes. Read the result through the resolved agent:

```bash
herdr agent get reviewer
herdr agent read reviewer --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

If a wait fails or returns `blocked`, inspect `agent get` and `agent read` before deciding what input to send. A timeout or stalled response does not prove the prompt was never delivered; do not blindly submit it again. Use the pane surface only when raw terminal control is intentional.

## Run an ordinary command in another pane

Create a sibling pane with the same geometry rule, preserve the caller's working directory, and keep user focus unchanged:

```bash
herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd "$PWD" --no-focus
```

Read the new pane ID from `.result.pane.pane_id`, then run and inspect the command:

```bash
herdr pane run <returned-pane-id> "just test"
herdr pane wait-output <returned-pane-id> --match "test result" --timeout 120000
herdr pane read <returned-pane-id> --source recent-unwrapped --lines 120
```

`pane run` queues command text and Enter together; success acknowledges admission, not command execution. On macOS, `pane run` and `agent start` reject a command that exceeds the terminal's current canonical line-input limit before queuing it. Wait for the interactive shell prompt before retrying. The check covers this submission, not an earlier incomplete line or a later terminal-mode change. `pane wait-output` searches the selected snapshot immediately, so output that already exists can match. Use `--match <text>` for a literal substring or `--regex <pattern>` for a Rust regular expression. Omitting `--timeout` allows an indefinite wait.

Use the read source that matches the task:

- `visible`: the currently rendered viewport.
- `recent`: recent rendered output, including soft wraps.
- `recent-unwrapped`: recent output with soft wraps joined; prefer it for logs and transcripts.
- `detection`: the plain-text bottom-buffer snapshot used for agent detection.

Use `--format ansi` when colors and terminal styling are evidence. Otherwise use text.

`--lines` asks Herdr for more rows from the pane's available screen and host scrollback. Alternate-screen rows do not enter ordinary host scrollback. For supported idle agents, Herdr can collect application-owned history and restore the viewport afterward, but not every application or response can be recovered this way.

If a larger recent read still does not reveal the completed response, ask the agent to write it as Markdown in a temporary directory and reply only with the file path, then read that file on the same machine. Use this only as a fallback; do not request file output in the initial prompt.

## Safety and coordination rules

- Use `--no-focus` for background work unless the user asked to switch context.
- Use `--current`, an explicit pane ID, or a unique agent name. Do not rely on another client's focused pane.
- Parse IDs from JSON responses. Do not derive them from sidebar order or examples.
- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes, or sessions you did not create unless the user explicitly asked. Ordinary CLI/API closes do not inherit the TUI's last-pane confirmation. `workspace close --group` closes the primary workspace and its linked worktree workspaces; never add it merely to bypass `workspace_group_close_required`.
- Use `--trust-repository` only after the user has verified the repository. It grants per-request Git trust; it is not a routine retry for a failed worktree command.
- Client and server versions can differ after an update. Check `herdr status` before relying on new server features. A missing method is not permission to stop or upgrade a server.
- Never run `herdr server stop` from an active session unless the user explicitly intends to stop the server and its pane processes.
- Never kill the main Herdr process. Use named test sessions for experiments that need an isolated server.
- CLI server errors are JSON on stderr with exit status 1. CLI syntax errors exit with status 2.

# tools

the main session is the orchestrator. it discusses, decides, delegates and reviews. anything that would fill its context (reading many files, research, implementing, long command output) goes to a worker in a herdr pane. only the worker's short reply comes back.

this is skogix asking, once, for every session: delegating to herdr workers is allowed without asking again.

## delegate: one task, one worktree, one worker

tested 2026-10-17, herdr 0.9.5.

```bash
b=<branch>; p=/home/skogix/skogai/.skogai/worktrees/$b
wt switch -c $b --no-cd -y
pane=$(herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd $p --no-focus | jq -r .result.pane.pane_id)
sleep 2; herdr pane run $pane "claude --permission-mode auto"
sleep 8; herdr agent rename $pane $b
herdr agent prompt $b "<task>" --wait --timeout 600000
herdr agent read $b --source recent-unwrapped --lines 40
```

- `herdr agent start` fails with `agent_pane_busy` on fish panes: atuin sits in the shell's foreground group. use `pane run` + `agent rename` instead; herdr detects claude by itself.
- `--permission-mode auto` so the worker doesn't stop for every shell command.
- the prompt says what to do, which files it may touch, to commit with an explicit `git commit -m` and to reply with one line (hash + what changed). the worker's context pays for the work, not ours.
- `--wait` returns on idle, done or blocked. on `blocked`, `agent read` and ask skogix before answering it.
- a timeout doesn't mean the prompt was lost. read before re-sending.

## review and land

```bash
git -C $p log --oneline master..HEAD
git -C $p diff --stat master...HEAD
wt -C $p merge -y            # squash into master, removes worktree + branch
wt -C $p merge -y --no-squash
herdr pane close $pane       # only panes we created
```

`wt merge` without `-m` uses the commit generator in `~/.config/worktrunk/config.toml` (`aichat -m ollama:llama3.2`). its messages come out quoted or nonsense, so workers commit with their own message and we merge with `--no-squash`, or squash and fix the message.

details: [TOOLS-wt.md](TOOLS-wt.md).

## herdr plugin actions (for skogix)

`herdr plugin action invoke <open|open-current|open-with-remotes|merge|merge-no-squash|remove> --plugin worktrunk` opens an interactive picker pane. it logs "succeeded" when the pane opens, not when the work is done. the orchestrator uses `wt` directly.

## reference

- `herdr --skill`: full herdr agent guide (ids, states, read sources, safety rules)
- `herdr <group>` with no subcommand lists commands. never run bare `herdr`.

# wt (worktrunk)

worktree manager. orchestrator stays put; workers live in worktrees.

## layout

worktrees live under `<repo>/.skogai/worktrees/<branch>` (`/` in branch becomes `-`), set by `worktree-path` in `~/.config/worktrunk/config.toml`.

## create without cd

```sh
wt switch --create feat-x --no-cd             # new branch + worktree off default branch
wt switch -c feat-x -b dev --no-cd            # base on another branch
wt switch -c feat-x --no-cd -x claude -- 'do the thing'   # spawn a program in it; shell stays
```

`--no-cd` only affects the shell. hooks and `-x` still run in the worktree.

## target a worktree

global `-C <path>` runs any command as if from that path:

```sh
wt -C .skogai/worktrees/feat-x step diff
wt -C .skogai/worktrees/feat-x merge -y
```

## list

```sh
wt list                   # table
wt list --format json     # for parsing
wt list --branches        # include branches without worktrees
wt list --full            # ci status + llm summaries
```

## merge

merges the *current* branch into target (default branch): commit → squash → rebase → hooks → fast-forward → remove worktree.

```sh
wt merge                  # squash into one commit, remove worktree
wt merge --no-squash      # keep branch history
wt merge --no-remove      # keep the worktree after merge
wt merge --stage tracked  # stage: all (default) | tracked | none
wt merge -y               # skip approval prompts
wt merge dev              # target another branch
```

also: `--no-commit`, `--no-rebase`, `--no-ff`, `--no-hooks`, `--format json`.

## remove

```sh
wt remove                          # current worktree; deletes branch if merged
wt remove feat-x feat-y            # by branch
wt remove --no-delete-branch feat-x
wt remove -D feat-x                # delete unmerged branch too
wt remove -f feat-x                # remove even if dirty
```

runs in background by default; `--foreground` to block.

## step

the pieces of `wt merge`, run by hand.

```sh
wt step commit                     # stage + commit, llm-generated message
wt step commit --stage none        # commit only what's in the index
wt step commit --dry-run           # preview message
wt step diff                       # everything since branching (committed, staged, unstaged, untracked)
wt step diff -- --stat             # extra args go to git diff
wt step squash | rebase | push     # rest of the merge pipeline
```

# tools

the main session is the orchestrator. it discusses, decides, delegates and reviews. anything that would fill its context (reading many files, research, implementing, long command output) goes to a worker in a herdr pane. only the worker's short reply comes back.

this is skogix asking, once, for every session: delegating to herdr workers is allowed without asking again.

## delegate: one task, one worktree, one worker

tested 2026-10-17, herdr 0.9.5.

```bash
b=<branch>; p=/home/skogix/skogai/.skogai/worktrees/$b
wt switch -c $b --no-cd -y
pane=$(herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd $p --no-focus | jq -r .result.pane.pane_id)
sleep 2; herdr pane run $pane "claude --permission-mode auto"
sleep 8; herdr agent rename $pane $b
herdr agent prompt $b "<task>" --wait --timeout 600000
herdr agent read $b --source recent-unwrapped --lines 40
```

- `herdr agent start` fails with `agent_pane_busy` on fish panes: atuin sits in the shell's foreground group. use `pane run` + `agent rename` instead; herdr detects claude by itself.

- `--wait` returns on idle, done or blocked. on `blocked`, `agent read` and ask skogix before answering it.
- a timeout doesn't mean the prompt was lost. read before re-sending.

# tools

the main session is the orchestrator. it discusses, decides, delegates and reviews. anything that would fill its context (reading many files, research, implementing, long command output) goes to a worker in a herdr pane. only the worker's short reply comes back.

this is skogix asking, once, for every session: delegating to herdr workers is allowed without asking again.

## delegate: one task, one worktree, one worker

tested 2026-10-17, herdr 0.9.5.

```bash
b=<branch>; p=/home/skogix/skogai/.skogai/worktrees/$b
wt switch -c $b --no-cd -y
pane=$(herdr pane split --current --direction right --cwd $p --no-focus | jq -r .result.pane.pane_id)
sleep 2; herdr pane run $pane "claude --permission-mode auto"
sleep 8; herdr agent rename $pane $b
herdr agent prompt $b "<task>" --wait --timeout 600000
herdr agent read $b --source recent-unwrapped --lines 40
```

- `herdr agent start` fails with `agent_pane_busy` on fish panes: atuin sits in the shell's foreground group. use `pane run` + `agent rename` instead; herdr detects claude by itself.
- `--permission-mode auto` so the worker doesn't stop for every shell command.
- the prompt says what to do, which files it may touch, to commit with an explicit `git commit -m` and to reply with one line (hash + what changed). the worker's context pays for the work, not ours.
- `--wait` returns on idle, done or blocked. on `blocked`, `agent read` and ask skogix before answering it.
- a timeout doesn't mean the prompt was lost. read before re-sending.

## review and land

```bash
git -C $p log --oneline master..HEAD
git -C $p diff --stat master...HEAD
herdr pane close $pane                            # only panes we created
wt -C $p merge -y --no-squash --stage none        # keeps the worker's commits
```

- `--stage none`: the skogai-core Stop hook writes the worker's turns into `.skogai/journal.md` in its worktree. the default `--stage all` would commit that into master.
- that same journal change blocks the worktree removal after merge. TODO.md decides what happens to it.

`wt merge` uses the commit generator in `~/.config/worktrunk/config.toml` (`aichat -m ollama:llama3.2`). its messages come out quoted or nonsense (`33df31e`), so workers commit with their own message and we merge with `--no-squash`.

details: [TOOLS-wt.md](TOOLS-wt.md).

## herdr plugin actions (for skogix)

`herdr plugin action invoke <open|open-current|open-with-remotes|merge|merge-no-squash|remove> --plugin worktrunk` opens an interactive picker pane. it logs "succeeded" when the pane opens, not when the work is done. the orchestrator uses `wt` directly.

## reference

- `herdr --skill`: full herdr agent guide (ids, states, read sources, safety rules)
- `herdr <group>` with no subcommand lists commands. never run bare `herdr`.

---

# type

a type defines a kind of thing. its definition is `type/<name>.md`, its instances live in `type/<name>/`, and `type/<name>.schema.json`, when there is one, is the schema for those instances. so [type.schema.json](type.schema.json) is the schema for every type definition.

## base

every instance of every type has the okf base. okf requires only `type`; the rest is optional:

- **identity**: `type`, `title`, `description`.
- **provenance**: `sources[]`, `usage_window`.
- **trust**: `generated: {by, at}`, `verified[]`.
- **lifecycle**: `status`, `stale_after`.

## definition

every type states:

- **type**: `type`.
- **title**: its name. instances carry it as their `type` in frontmatter.
- **fields**: the frontmatter every instance must have, beyond `type`.
- **owns**: the paths each instance creates and manages fully. every path has exactly one owner.
- **writes**: the paths each instance modifies without owning them.
- **watches**: the paths each instance reads and wants to know about when they change.

`<name>` in a path is the instance's name. a path ending in `/` is a folder.

## check

- a file with no owner is untyped: an error.
- a file with two owners is a conflict: an error.
- ownership is one step. `type` owns `type/tool.md`; `tool` owns `type/tool/gita.md`. `type` never owns what is under `type/tool/`.
- `writes` and `watches` can overlap freely.

`type` is itself a type: every `type/<name>.md` is an instance of it, including this file.

---
type: type
title: config
description: key/value settings, folded across the base, global and local layers.
fields: [type, title]
owns: [config]
---

# config

a config is a [git config](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#_configuration_file) file of `section.key = value` pairs, read and written with `skogai config`.

## layers

folded in order, later wins:

1. **base**: `config` in dash. the defaults.
2. **global**: `~/.skogai/config`, or `$SKOGAI_GLOBAL_CONFIG`.
3. **local**: `<repo>/.skogai/config`, or `$SKOGAI_LOCAL_CONFIG`.
4. **file**: with `--file x.md` (repeatable), the frontmatter of `x.md`, then of `x.local.md`. nested keys flatten to `a.b.c`, `_` reads as `-`, and `--scope s` mounts them under `s.`. needs `yq`.
5. **env**: key `a.b-c` reads env `SKOGAI_A_BC`, which overrides every layer. `.` is a relation and becomes `_`; `-` is part of a name and is dropped.

## commands

- `skogai config get <key> [--show-origin] [--file x.md]... [--scope s]`: exit `1` if unset, `2` if a layer can't be read. a list prints one item per line.
- `skogai config set <key> <value> [--global | --file x.md [--scope s]]`: writes local unless `--global`. `--file` writes `x.local.md`, never `x.md`; the value is read as yaml.
- `skogai config unset <key> [--global | --file x.md [--scope s]]`
- `skogai config list [--show-origin] [--file x.md]... [--scope s]`: a list prints one line per item.
- `skogai config env [--file x.md]... [--scope s]`: the resolved config as `export` lines, for `mise` `_.source` or `eval`. a list's items are newline-separated.
- `skogai config files [--file x.md]...`: the path of each layer, and whether it exists.

## merge

every key is replaced by the later layer. a key set twice in one layer resolves to its last value.

in a file layer, a frontmatter list is one value, replaced whole. `null` (`~`) removes the key, so it falls through to the default.

## keys

- `stage.on-stop`, `commit.on-stop`, `merge.on-stop`: git automation on stop.
- `stage.on-user-prompt-submit`, `commit.on-user-prompt-submit`, `merge.on-user-prompt-submit`: git automation on prompt submit.

# event

an event is something that happened, such as a turn ending or a tool about to run. each time it happens, one row is appended to the event log. rows are never edited; the log as a whole is temporary and can be deleted.

an event `<name>` owns:

- `type/event/<name>.md`: the instance. it says what happened and when it fires.
- `type/event/<name>.schema.json`: its rows. it narrows the row in [event.schema.json](event.schema.json) to this event's `input`.
- `scripts/event/<name>.sh`: what runs when it happens.

- **enabled**: optional. an event runs only when this is `true`. missing, or no instance at all, is off.

## the row

one json object per line in `.skogai/logs/event.jsonl`:

- **ts**: when it happened, utc, to the millisecond.
- **event**: the instance's `title`.
- **action**: optional, what the script did, when it did more than record the row.
- **input**: everything the event came with, unchanged. `$defs/input` in the schema lists the fields every event shares; `type/event/<name>.schema.json` adds its own and says which are required.

## the script

`scripts/event/<name>.sh` gets the event's `input` and appends exactly one row. it may answer: go on, stop with a reason, or a structured answer the event's source understands. when it can't run, it says so and lets the event go on, so a broken script never stops work.

## defaults

no event is on. the log path is the base config key `event.log-path`.

type: type
title: router
description: a file that points to other files, so an agent loads only what the task needs.
status: draft
fields: [type, title]
owns: [<name>/SKOGAI.md, <name>/CLAUDE.md]

# router

a router routes, it does not hold content. its body is one `<routes>` block: the frontmatter `type` names the block, as `router` names `<routes>`.

```markdown
---
type: router
title: dash-skogai
---

<routes>

- @type/index.md - small index, loaded with the router
- tmp/ - untyped or undecided, read when needed

</routes>
```

- **entries**: one per line, `- <path> [- <description>]`. the description lets an agent decide without opening the file.
- **`@path`**: loaded with the router. use it for small routers and indexes.
- **plain path**: listed, read on demand. use it for anything with real content.
- **no transitive bloat**: a router never `@`-links a file that itself `@`-links content. that loads everything below it.
- **one step**: each router points to the next level, never to everything.

## CLAUDE.md

claude code loads only `CLAUDE.md`, never `SKOGAI.md`. so each router also owns the `CLAUDE.md` next to it, and that file is derived: its whole content is

```markdown
@SKOGAI.md
```

it is never hand-edited, and `check` regenerates and compares it. routes go in `SKOGAI.md`, not in `CLAUDE.md`.

the source this was folded from is [tmp/routing](../tmp/routing/README.md).

# skogai

the cli that turns dash into a dot. it is a function over values: `check` and `plan` are pure, and `apply` is the only writer.

## values

- **dash**: type definitions and functions, named by ref and resolved to a commit at use.
- **layers**: `base` (dash@ref), `global` (`~/.skogai`), `local` (`<repo>/.skogai`). key/value settings use [config](../config.md).
- **resolved**: `fold(merge, [base, global, local])`, later layer wins.
- **dot**: the resolved value written to disk, a closed union of skogai types.

## commands

### `skogai config`

implemented in `bin/skogai`. see [config](../config.md).

### `skogai check [<dot>]`

pure. reports type errors, writes nothing.

1. runs `okn validate` on the dot.
2. every file has exactly one owner (see [type](../type.md#check)).
3. every `type` tag is a case dash defines, and the file has that case's `fields`.
4. every derived file equals its regeneration.

prints the dash ref and the commit it resolved to.

### `skogai resolve [<dot>]`

pure. prints the resolved value, and for each entry the layer it came from.

### `skogai plan [<dot>]`

pure. prints the patch `apply` would make, as a git diff. an empty patch means the dot is already up to date.

### `skogai apply [<dot>] [<patch>]`

the only writer. applies `<patch>`, or the output of `plan` if none is given, with `git apply`.

- idempotent: after `apply`, `plan` is empty.
- init is `apply` on an empty dot.
- moving to a newer dash is changing the ref, then `plan` and `apply`.

## conventions

- `<dot>` defaults to `./.skogai`.
- output goes to stdout, diagnostics to stderr.
- exit `0`: clean or empty patch. `1`: type errors or a non-empty patch. `2`: usage or internal error.
- `--json` on every command, for machine output.
- anything okn already does (list, search, view, validate) is called through okn, not rebuilt.

## open

see [TODO](../../TODO.md): where the dash ref is recorded, merge semantics per field, and how a type declares a derived file.

We can't prove where `12:46:8D:0C:77:F7` came from. My best guess is that it's a **randomized MAC from an earlier setup of this machine**: a previous install, or an old Wi-Fi adapter or connection. It isn't from anything on this box right now.

**Evidence:**
- `0x12` has the locally-administered bit set, so this is a generated MAC, not a hardware one. NetworkManager and iwd produce these for Wi-Fi by default.
- It announced the hostname `skogix-workstation`, so something running as this machine requested it.
- Today the box has only `enp0s31f6` (`60:45:…`, the real MAC on the board) and `tailscale0`. There's no Wi-Fi interface and no cloned-MAC setting in NetworkManager.
- The journal (about 20 boots back) never mentions it, and nothing in `/etc/systemd/network` or the NM state uses it.
- The router lists it with lease "Permanent". That's just how it shows reserved entries; it doesn't mean the device is online.

So it's a leftover. Because the reservation is tied to a MAC that no longer exists, the wired NIC fell back to a normal pool address, `.3`.

**Fix that keeps your chosen IP:** edit the existing reservation from `12:46:8D:0C:77:F7` to `60:45:CB:A9:11:91` and keep `10.10.4.5`. The workstation moves from `.3` to `.5` at its next lease renewal, or straight away if you reconnect.

Tailscale is already running on this box, which helps with the remote part later.

Shall I make that edit and save it?

Now, to manage "most things" remotely with Tailscale as the transport, here's what's needed and what's still missing. Your WAN is CGNAT, so Tailscale (outbound) is the right and really the only choice.

## The pieces

**1. Tailscale running *on* pfSense** — the key missing one.
Your tailnet shows `brg-skogix-pfs` offline 252 days. This rebuilt VM needs the **Tailscale package** (System → Package Manager) installed and logged into your headscale tailnet. Then pfSense's GUI (443) and SSH (22) are reachable from any tailnet node, anywhere, no port-forward.

**2. Subnet routes advertised** — so you reach the LANs, not just the firewall.
In the Tailscale package, enable **Advertise Routes** for `10.10.5.0/24` (and `10.10.4.0/24` if you want the TP-Link side too), and turn on IP forwarding. Then approve those routes on the headscale side. This lets a remote laptop hit any host behind pfSense.

**3. Firewall rule on the Tailscale interface** — allow management traffic in. The package usually adds a default allow; worth confirming.

**4. A lockout-proof fallback** — before tightening anything, keep console/serial access to the VM host, so a bad firewall rule can't strand you. I'd also add your SSH **public key** to the pfSense admin user so access doesn't depend only on the password.

**5. The WoL relay (your original goal)** — pfSense is the always-on box. Enable **Services → Wake-on-LAN**, then over Tailscale you tell pfSense to send the magic packet to the workstation's wired MAC `60:45:CB:A9:11:91`. That closes the loop from the start of this thread.

Tailscale-on-pfSense → advertise routes → verify remote GUI/SSH → then WoL service → then harden (SSH key, firewall).

Got it all. The intended control server is in your history: **`https://hs.aldervall.se`** (headscale). Here's the environment picture for this workstation — no changes made, all read-only.

## What's actually wrong

**1. This workstation's Tailscale is logged out AND pointed at the wrong server.**
- `tailscaled` is active+enabled, but the backend says *"Logged out. Log in at login.tailscale.com"*.
- Its configured `ControlURL` is `https://controlplane.tailscale.com` — **public Tailscale**, not your headscale.
- Result: no `100.64.x` address on `tailscale0` (only link-local v6). **The workstation is not on the headscale tailnet via its own daemon.**

**2. My earlier "ping worked from the workstation" was misleading.**
- Route to `100.64.0.19` is `via 10.10.4.1` (the default gateway), **not** `tailscale0`. So it reached pfSense's tailnet IP purely through LAN routing (pfSense is genuinely on the tailnet and owns that IP locally). It never proved the workstation's own Tailscale works — because it doesn't right now.

**3. cloudflared is crash-looping — this is your "cloudflare in the middle."**
- `cloudflared.service` runs `tunnel run --token-file /etc/cloudflared/token`, but `/etc/cloudflared/` is **empty** — no token. It exits 255 and systemd restarts it every ~5s. **NRestarts = 1887** and climbing.
- Separately, a *working* named tunnel **`skogai`** (PID 990488, uid 165531) has been up 2h42m. So you have one good tunnel and one broken duplicate unit spamming restarts.

**4. Leftover tailscale policy routing** (`ip rule` fwmark 0x80000 + table 52, currently empty) sits there while logged out — harmless but it's the "routing weirdly" residue.

**5. DNS** is on Cloudflare (1.1.1.1/1.0.0.1) via systemd-resolved. Fine, just noting it's Cloudflare too.

## Fixes (all need sudo — you run them)

```
# 1. Put the workstation back on the real tailnet (from your history):
sudo tailscale up --login-server https://hs.aldervall.se --accept-routes --ssh

# 2. Stop the broken crash-loop unit (keep the working "skogai" tunnel):
sudo systemctl disable --now cloudflared
#    …or drop the missing token into /etc/cloudflared/token if you want that unit.

# 3. (on headscale) approve pfSense's subnet route so remote nodes reach the LAN:
headscale routes list           # find 10.10.5.0/24 for skogix-pfsense
headscale routes enable -r <id>
```

After #1, this box gets `100.64.0.25` for real and `ssh admin@100.64.0.19` works over the tunnel, not just via LAN. #2 stops the 1887-restart noise. #3 is what finally exposes everything behind pfSense to remote nodes.

# everything in it afterwards was produced by this run.
#
#   echo "say pong" | bin/agent
#   echo "list files" | SETUP=tools TOOLS=Bash bin/agent
#   echo "hi" | SETUP=loadout LOADOUT=vanilla bin/agent
#
# A setup is a layer on top of setups/baseline (see bin/layers). Per layer, in order:
#   settings.json            deep-merged into config/settings.json (later keys win)
#   config/                  copied over the config dir (CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR)
#   work/                    copied over the working dir (CLAUDE.md, .claude/, fixtures)
#   plugin-dirs              one path per line, each passed as --plugin-dir
#   system-prompt.md         --system-prompt-file
#   append-system-prompt.md  --append-system-prompt-file
# The prompt files come from the last layer that has either of them, so a setup
# with only append-system-prompt.md keeps Claude Code's default prompt.
# LOADOUT sets the active profile in the sandbox's loadout store.
set -euo pipefail
root=$(cd "$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$0")")/.." && pwd)

: "${SETUP:=baseline}"
: "${MODEL:=haiku}"
: "${TOOLS:=}"
: "${OUTPUT:=text}"
: "${SANDBOX_ROOT:=/tmp/claude-code}"
export MAX_THINKING_TOKENS="${MAX_THINKING_TOKENS:-0}"

mapfile -t layers < <("$root/bin/layers" "$SETUP")
box="${BOX:-$SANDBOX_ROOT/$SETUP}"

if [[ ${KEEP:-0} != 1 || ! -d $box ]]; then
  rm -rf "$box"
  mkdir -p "$box/config" "$box/work"
  ln -s "$HOME/.claude/.credentials.json" "$box/config/.credentials.json"
  echo '{}' > "$box/config/settings.json"
  for layer in "${layers[@]}"; do
    if [[ -f $layer/settings.json ]]; then
      jq -s '.[0] * .[1]' "$box/config/settings.json" "$layer/settings.json" > "$box/config/settings.json.new"
      mv "$box/config/settings.json.new" "$box/config/settings.json"
    fi
    [[ -d $layer/config ]] && cp -aL "$layer/config/." "$box/config/"
    [[ -d $layer/work ]] && cp -aL "$layer/work/." "$box/work/"
  done
fi

if [[ -n ${LOADOUT:-} ]]; then
  for store in "$box"/config/plugins/store/loadout_*.json; do
    [[ -f $store ]] || continue
    jq -e --arg p "$LOADOUT" 'any(.profiles[]; .name == $p)' "$store" >/dev/null \
      || { echo "LOADOUT=$LOADOUT: no such profile in $store" >&2; exit 1; }
    jq --arg p "$LOADOUT" '.active = $p' "$store" > "$store.new" && mv "$store.new" "$store"
  done
fi

export CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR="$box/config"
cd "$box/work"

args=(
  -p
  --model "$MODEL"
  --tools "$TOOLS"
  --strict-mcp-config
  --disable-slash-commands
  --output-format "$OUTPUT"
)
prompts=
for layer in "${layers[@]}"; do
  [[ -f $layer/system-prompt.md || -f $layer/append-system-prompt.md ]] && prompts=$layer
  if [[ -f $layer/plugin-dirs ]]; then
    while read -r dir; do
      [[ -n $dir ]] && args+=(--plugin-dir "${dir/#\~/$HOME}")
    done < "$layer/plugin-dirs"
  fi
done
[[ -n $prompts && -f $prompts/system-prompt.md ]] && args+=(--system-prompt-file "$prompts/system-prompt.md")
[[ -n $prompts && -f $prompts/append-system-prompt.md ]] && args+=(--append-system-prompt-file "$prompts/append-system-prompt.md")
[[ $OUTPUT == stream-json ]] && args+=(--verbose)

exec claude "${args[@]}" "$@"
